metadata.title: A Cross-national Study of Mathematics Anxiety

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses PISA 2012 Student Questionnaire data and applies PISA sampling weights (SW) and design effects (DE) to obtain representative estimates for the selected Asia–Pacific economies. The analytic sample is restricted to students who completed the questionnaire form containing the main anxiety items (excluding Form-A) and to the five selected economies. The authors do not report a specific weight variable name (e.g., W_FSTUWT), but they explicitly state that sampling weights and design effects procedures were used following the PISA 2012 User Guide. No replicate-weight method (e.g., BRR/jackknife) is described, and the reported analyses are primarily descriptive comparisons, partial correlations, and multiple linear regressions rather than PV-based achievement modeling.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The dependent variable is mathematics anxiety constructed from six PISA 2012 attitude items (ST42Q01–ST42Q06) via factor analysis, not a cognitive achievement score with PISA plausible values. Because the study focuses on an attitude factor rather than PV-based achievement, PV handling is not applicable. The manuscript also does not describe any explicit missing-data procedure for questionnaire items (e.g., complete-case exclusion or imputation), so missing-data handling is treated as not reported.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Used PISA 2012 Student Questionnaire data for five Asia–Pacific economies selected as top/bottom mathematics achievement performers. Excluded students who completed Form-A because Form-A does not include the main anxiety variable ST42 for the mathematics anxiety analysis. After this questionnaire-form restriction, the effective sample size is 17,284 students. The study then constructs the mathematics anxiety factor from the 10 ST42 attitude items via factor analysis and focuses on the first factor (M-Anxiety) mainly related to six items.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2012 Student Questionnaire (15-year-olds) — Mathematics anxiety (ST42 factor)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Partial correlations (controlling gender and ESCS): Test-score r ranges from -0.22 to -0.42 (all p<0.001); Interests r ranges from -0.10 to -0.42 (all p<0.001); Familiarity r ranges from -0.14 to -0.32 (all p<0.001). Multiple regression R Square: Indonesia 0.04, Korea 0.07, Malaysia 0.04, Shanghai 0.17, Singapore 0.13. Regression coefficient: S_Efforts negative and significant in all economies (e.g., Shanghai -0.27***; Singapore -0.26***).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2012 Student Questionnaire the study leveraged mathematics test score, interest in mathematics, familiarity with math terms, student study efforts, and gender (as a controlled factor) to analyze mathematics anxiety, finding that mathematics anxiety is consistently negatively associated with achievement-related and self-reported learning variables and that student study efforts are the only consistently significant predictor across all five economies. This indicates that interventions that strengthen students’ engagement with math and sustained study effort may reduce mathematics anxiety, though the study is correlational and does not establish causal effects.

data.outcome_summary: This cross-national study uses PISA 2012 Student Questionnaire data for 15-year-old students from five Asia–Pacific economies (Indonesia, Korea, Malaysia, China-Shanghai, and Singapore; total N=17,284 after excluding Form-A students). Mathematics anxiety is operationalized as a factor derived from PISA ST42 attitude items, focusing on the M-Anxiety factor (six items). The study reports weighted descriptive comparisons and then uses partial correlations (controlling gender and ESCS) and multiple linear regressions to relate M-Anxiety to student, teacher, and peer-related constructs. Across all economies, M-Anxiety shows significant negative relationships with mathematics test score, interests, and familiarity (e.g., test-score correlations as low as r=-0.42, p<0.001). In regressions, student study efforts (S_Efforts) is the only factor significant across all five economies (e.g., Shanghai -0.27***; Singapore -0.26***), while teacher and peer variables show weak or non-uniform effects. Limitations include the absence of an explicit missing-data strategy and the fact that the analysis is not a machine-learning predictive pipeline.
